title: The House Hunting Checklist: How to Actually Find a Rental in India
seoTitle: House Hunting Checklist for Renting in India
description: A phase-by-phase checklist for renting in India: what to budget, how to read a listing, what to check on the visit, and what to settle before you pay.
excerpt: Most people inspect the flat carefully and the commute not at all. Here is the full process, from budgeting to possession day, with the physical checks that matter.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: People who have looked at a lot of flats in a lot of heat

hero.alt: Futuristic illustration of a holographic lens scanning a row of houses, one glowing jade with check marks around it

faq.q: How many flats should I see before deciding?
faq.a: Five or six visits is usually enough to know what your money buys in that area, and beyond about eight the flats start blurring into each other. Quality of attention matters more than quantity — one weekday-evening visit tells you more than three rushed Sunday ones. If nothing on a shortlist of six works, the problem is usually the budget or the area, not the sample size.

faq.q: What is the single most important thing to check during a flat visit?
faq.a: Water. Run every tap fully, check the pressure, and then ask about the supply — the source, the hours it comes, the tank capacity and what happens in summer. Supply is scheduled rather than constant in much of India, so a tap that works at 3pm on a Sunday proves very little on its own. It is the one issue you cannot fix, cannot negotiate around, and will think about every single day.

faq.q: Should I visit a flat more than once?
faq.a: For your final one or two options, yes. Come back at the hour you would actually be home, ideally on a weekday evening. Light, noise, traffic, parking pressure and how safe the last stretch of road feels all change completely between a Sunday afternoon and a Wednesday at 9pm.

faq.q: How do I spot seepage or damp before I sign?
faq.a: Look at ceiling corners, the wall around every window frame, behind the toilet and under the kitchen sink. A faint brown or yellow ring with a darker edge, or paint that is puffed and lifting, is water. One patch of fresh white paint on an otherwise ageing ceiling is a repair worth asking about. Damp also has a smell — earthy and slightly sour in a closed room.

faq.q: Is it worth paying a token amount to hold a flat?
faq.a: Sometimes, if you are genuinely certain and the market is moving fast. But token amounts are frequently not refunded in practice, whatever was said verbally. If you pay one, get the amount, the date, what it is for and the refund condition in writing first — even a message thread is better than nothing.

faq.q: How much should I budget beyond the rent itself?
faq.a: Plan for the deposit and advance rent up front, plus agreement and stamp costs, possible painting charges and movers. Monthly, add maintenance, electricity, water, parking, internet and — the one most people forget — the actual cost of your commute twice a day. A cheaper flat that is forty minutes further away is often not cheaper at all.

body:
Meera took a flat in Chennai in April. She saw it at eleven on a Tuesday morning, liked the light, liked the landlord, and paid a token amount that evening because two other people were "also looking." Everyone says that. She believed it anyway.

What she regretted six weeks later wasn't the rent. It was the road. Her office was nine kilometres away, which sounds like nothing until you do it at 9am on a stretch that funnels into a single flyover. Google Maps said twenty-two minutes at noon. It was fifty-five to seventy in the morning, every morning, and about the same coming back. She'd inspected the flat carefully and never once inspected the journey.

That's the pattern. People examine the wrong thing closely and the right thing not at all. They'll open every cupboard and forget to open a tap.

## Why everyone rushes, and why it costs

House hunting in India runs on manufactured urgency. There's usually someone else looking. Sometimes that's true. Often it's the oldest line in the business, and it works because the alternative — another three weekends of autos, missed calls and stairs in 38-degree heat — is genuinely miserable.

So people compress a decision they'll live inside for eleven months into forty minutes on a Sunday afternoon, then discover the water comes for two hours a day, or the "power backup" runs one light and a fan, or the bedroom faces west and is unusable until 8pm in May.

None of that shows up in photographs. All of it shows up in your life. The fix isn't to be cleverer during the visit — it's to do the work *before* it, so the visit only has to answer a few specific questions. Here's the whole process, in five phases.

## Phase 1: Before you look at a single listing

### Budget the real number, not the rent

Rent is the headline, not the cost. Before you filter anything, write down what actually leaves your account every month:

| Line item | What to establish before you shortlist |
| --- | --- |
| Rent | The number you can pay on the 5th of a bad month, not a good one |
| Maintenance | Fixed or per square foot? Monthly or quarterly? Who collects it? |
| Electricity | Is the meter separate and in your name, or split by the owner? |
| Water | Included, metered, or tanker-dependent in summer? |
| Parking | Charged separately in many buildings. Two-wheeler and car differ |
| Internet | Which providers actually service that building |
| Commute | Fuel or fares, twice a day, twenty-two days a month |

That last row is the one people leave out, and it's often the size of a maintenance bill. A flat that's two thousand cheaper but forty minutes further away is not cheaper.

Then there's day-one money — deposit, advance rent, agreement cost, painting charges, movers. We've written separately on [the costs that don't appear in the rent figure](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) and on [how deposits work and how to get yours back](/blog/security-deposits-in-india), because they need more room than a checklist gives them.

### Separate non-negotiables from preferences

Write two lists. Be honest and be short.

Non-negotiables are things that would make you move out. A commute ceiling. Ground-floor access for a parent who can't climb. A kitchen that fits your fridge. Nice-to-haves are everything else — the balcony, the modular kitchen, the gym nobody in the building uses. If your non-negotiable list has nine items on it, it isn't a list of non-negotiables, it's a wish. Cut it to four.

### Choose the area before you choose the flat

This is the highest-leverage step in the whole process, and almost nobody does it in the right order.

Most people browse flats, fall for one, then decide the area is fine because the flat is good. That's backwards. You can repaint a flat. You cannot move a road.

Do it the other way. Pick two or three areas that survive your commute test, then look at what's available inside them. Test the commute at the hour you'd actually travel — not on a Sunday, not at 2pm. If you can, do the journey once for real before you shortlist anything there. One evening, and it's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

[Why starting from a map beats starting from a list](/blog/why-maps-beat-lists-for-finding-a-home) goes into this properly. If you're looking in Chennai specifically, [a rundown of the areas and what each is actually like](/blog/best-areas-to-live-in-chennai) will save you a weekend.

## Phase 2: Shortlisting, and how to read a listing

A listing is a sales document. Read it like one.

**What's missing tells you more than what's there.** No photo of the bathroom usually means the bathroom is the problem. No photo of the kitchen platform means the platform is chipped or the sink is stained. No exterior shot means the building looks worse than the flat.

**Watch the angles.** Wide-angle lenses aren't a scandal — everyone uses them — but they make a small room look like a hall. Look for reference objects: if a double bed occupies half the frame and the room still looks huge, the lens is doing work. Count floor tiles if you can see them; a standard tile gives you a ruler. And look at what's just outside the window in every shot, because people frame around the thing they don't want you to see.

**Stale listings waste your weekends.** If the same flat has been up for months in a market where things move in days, either it's gone and nobody removed it, or something's wrong and everyone who visited found it. Ask a plain question when you call: is this still available, and when did someone last see it? A vague answer is an answer.

Shortlist five or six. Not fifteen. You'll stop seeing detail by the fourth visit anyway.

## Phase 3: The visit — what to physically check

Go with a plan. You have maybe twenty minutes of real attention before politeness takes over and you start nodding at everything. Bring someone — a second person notices what you don't, and is much harder to hurry.

### Water — do this first, always

Open the tap. Not a polite trickle — open it fully, in the kitchen and in every bathroom. Watch the pressure. Then flush the toilet and run the tap at the same time, and see what happens to the flow.

Then ask what the tap can't tell you, because supply in most Indian cities is scheduled rather than constant: when does water come and for how long, is it corporation line or borewell or tanker, what's the tank capacity, and who pays when tankers are needed in summer. Ask what happened last April.

Look at the water in a glass. Borewell water in some areas is hard enough to ruin a geyser in two years.

### Ventilation, direction and light

Stand in the middle of the flat and work out which way it faces. A west-facing bedroom collects the entire afternoon and holds it until midnight. East is gentle. North is the quiet win nobody asks for.

Then check cross-ventilation, which matters more than direction: are there windows on two different walls, or does all the air have one way in and no way out? Open everything and see whether anything moves. A flat with windows on one side only is a flat you'll air-condition all year. And notice what the windows open *into* — a window facing a two-foot shaft between buildings is a window in name only.

If you work days, the flat's midday brightness is irrelevant to you; you'll see this place at 7am and after 7pm. Look at what's blocking the windows, ask the watchman when the light goes, and if the flat matters enough, come back once in the evening. It's the most informative second visit you can make.

### Seepage — learn what it looks like

This is the defect that turns into a monsoon-long argument, and it hides in plain sight.

Look up. Ceiling corners, especially in the bathroom and under any flat above you. You're looking for a faint brown or yellow ring — like a coffee stain with a darker edge — or paint that's slightly puffed and lifting away from the surface. Fresh, suspiciously white paint in one corner of an otherwise ageing ceiling is a repair, not a coincidence.

Check around every window frame, particularly the side that catches driving rain, plus the wall behind the toilet and under the kitchen sink. Press a fingertip on any patch that looks off-colour; damp plaster gives slightly and feels cool.

And smell. A closed flat with a damp problem smells like it — earthy, slightly sour. If the windows were opened five minutes before you arrived, that's worth noticing too.

### The bathroom and kitchen

Bathrooms are where the money hides. Check that the floor slopes to the drain — pour a mug of water and watch where it goes. Check the geyser: is there one, does it work, how old, who replaces it. Check the flush actually stops. Look at the taps for a green-white crust, which is a hardness problem, not a cleaning problem.

Kitchen: run your hand along the platform edge for chips. Look under the sink for staining and for a trap that's been replaced with a bit of pipe. Check whether there's a point for a chimney or exhaust. Count the plug points, then count your appliances. Most old kitchens have two.

### Power, signal, lifts and the building itself

Power backup is a phrase, not a specification. Ask what it actually runs — the whole flat, or two lights and a fan? Generator or inverter, who maintains it, and is there a separate charge?

Take your phone out and check signal in every room, especially the bedroom. Plenty of newer buildings have thick walls and one bar. If you work from home, this is a non-negotiable disguised as a detail.

Then stop looking at the flat and look at the building. Walk the staircase, not just the lift. Is the stairwell lit? Rubbish on the landings? Does the lift have a working phone and a recent inspection sticker? Is the wiring in the common areas tidy or a nest?

A well-run building with an average flat beats a beautiful flat in a building nobody maintains. You'll share the second one's problems for eleven months.

### Parking and noise

Ask to be shown the exact parking slot, not "there's parking." Stand in it. Can you actually turn into it? Is it allotted or first-come? Does it flood?

Noise is the one the visit only half answers — you learn about the hour you visited and nothing else. Ask what's next door and above: a function hall, a school, a workshop, a generator, a road trucks use at night. Then come back at the time you'll actually be home. Ten minutes on the balcony at 9pm tells you more than the entire viewing did.

## Phase 4: The street, not just the flat

Once you're done inside, don't leave. Walk.

Walk the road to the nearest main junction and back. Notice the footpath, or the absence of one, and whether the last hundred metres to the door is lit — that's the stretch you'll do alone at night with bags.

Check what's genuinely near. "Everything is nearby" means nothing. What's the nearest thing you'd need at 10pm on a Tuesday — pharmacy, grocer, ATM, clinic — and how far is it *on foot*, not in a straight line? A shop 400 metres away with a railway line in between is a fifteen-minute walk.

Then ask about the monsoon story of the road. This one question — "how is this road in the rains?" — has saved more people than any other. Shopkeepers tell you the truth because they live with it. Look for the physical evidence too: a waterline stain on compound walls, doorsteps that have been raised, sandbags stacked in a corner in a dry month.

And come back after dark at least once, for one of your final two options. Streets change character at 9pm. Some get quiet and pleasant. Some get quiet and empty, which is different.

## Phase 5: Deciding, and what to lock down before you pay

By now you'll have two homes you like for different reasons and no clean way to compare them. Do it on paper — emotion loses to a table.

| Compare on | Home A | Home B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Real monthly cost (rent + maintenance + utilities + commute) | | |
| Door-to-door commute at your actual travel time | | |
| Water: source, hours, summer plan | | |
| Light and ventilation at the hours you're home | | |
| Building condition and how it's run | | |
| Non-negotiables met (out of your four) | | |
| Things that would annoy you daily | | |

Fill it in the same evening, while you still remember which flat had the good kitchen. Score the non-negotiables first. If a home fails one, it's out — that's what the word means.

Before any money changes hands, get the basics settled in writing, even as a message: rent, deposit and how it's refunded, maintenance and who pays it, notice period on both sides, who handles repairs, whether rent rises on renewal, and the possession date. Confirm you're dealing with the owner or someone genuinely authorised — a lot of trouble starts here, which is why [the warning signs of a rental scam](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) is its own article, along with [the questions worth asking before you commit](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) and [what belongs in the agreement](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india).

Then photograph everything on possession day. Every wall, every fitting, every existing crack and stain, meter readings included. Ten minutes with a phone camera has settled more deposit disputes than any clause ever will.

## The compact checklist

Print this, or keep it open on your phone.

**Before you search**
- Real monthly budget, including commute and maintenance
- Four non-negotiables, written down
- Two or three areas chosen and commute-tested at your actual hour
- Move-in cash total: deposit + advance + agreement + painting + movers

**Shortlisting**
- Is the bathroom photographed? The kitchen platform? The building exterior?
- Do the photos show what's outside the windows?
- Is the listing current — when did someone last see it?

**At the flat**
- Run every tap fully. Check pressure. Flush and run together
- Ask: water source, timing, tank size, summer/tanker plan, who pays
- Which way does it face? Windows on two walls or one?
- Ceiling corners, window frames, behind the toilet, under the sink — seepage
- Smell for damp. Look for one patch of fresh paint
- Bathroom floor slope, geyser, flush, tap crust
- Kitchen platform chips, plug points, exhaust provision
- Mobile signal in every room
- Power backup: what does it actually run, and what does it cost?
- Staircase, lift, common areas, water tank — the building, not the flat
- Stand in the actual parking slot
- Ask what's above and next door, then return at your own evening hour

**Outside**
- Walk to the main road and back. Is the last stretch lit?
- Pharmacy, grocer, ATM, clinic — walking distance, not straight-line
- Ask a shopkeeper how the road is in the rains
- Return once after dark

**Before paying**
- Comparison table filled in, non-negotiables scored first
- Rent, deposit, refund terms, maintenance, notice, repairs, renewal — in writing
- Verified you're dealing with the owner or an authorised person
- Photos of everything on possession day, meter readings included

## The mistakes people repeat

**Falling for the flat and rationalising the area.** If you catch yourself explaining why a bad commute is fine, stop. You're negotiating with yourself.

**Visiting only on Sunday afternoon.** The least representative hour of the week. Traffic is light, offices are shut, the building is quiet, and the light is at its best.

**Paying a token to "hold" it.** Sometimes reasonable, often not, and rarely refundable in practice. If you must, get the terms in writing before it leaves your account.

**Trusting "it will be fixed before you move in."** Sometimes it is. Frequently it isn't. If a repair matters, it goes in writing with a date, or it doesn't count.

## A few things that only come with practice

Go up one floor and down one, and look at the landings. Neighbours are half your experience of a home, and you're allowed to know something about them before you sign.

Ask who lived there before and why they left. The answer, or the hesitation, is informative.

If a place feels wrong and you can't say why, that's usually your nose registering damp or your ears registering a road. Go back and find it rather than dismissing it.

Rank your shortlist the same evening. By Thursday, every flat has merged into one composite flat with the best features of all of them, which does not exist.

## Where StayOnMap fits in this

Briefly, because a checklist shouldn't turn into a pitch.

Our homepage is a map rather than a list for exactly the Phase 1 reason above — it's built so you pick an area first and see what's inside it, rather than falling for a flat and working backwards to justify where it is.

Listings state rent, deposit and maintenance upfront, so the real monthly number is something you can work out before spending a Saturday travelling. There's no brokerage and you contact the owner directly, which mostly means asking your water and parking questions before the visit instead of during it. Each property page also shows what's genuinely near that home and how far, measured from that address rather than the neighbourhood in general.

It won't tell you whether the ceiling has a seepage stain. Nothing online will. That part still needs you, a Tuesday evening, and a working tap.

## In the end

A rental decision is made in an afternoon and lived with for a year. The gap between those two timescales is where the regret lives.

You don't need to be suspicious, or difficult, or to inspect a flat like a surveyor. You need to check the handful of things that are expensive to be wrong about — water, light, air, noise, the road, the building, the real monthly number — and check them before the momentum of "someone else is also looking" decides for you.

Meera's second flat, found four months later, was slightly smaller and marginally more expensive. Her commute went from an hour to fourteen minutes. She says it's the best trade she's ever made, and that she'd have found it the first time if she'd looked at the map before the photographs.
